H1.text: A final scoreboard tells you who won. A snapshot mid-match tells you who is pulling ahead.

H2.text: Chemistry has both numbers. One tells how far a reaction goes. One tells which way it will move.

H3.text: Aarav sits at his study table with a test paper at night. The question gives him just one number, K.

H4.text: It asks which way the mixture will move, and how much of each gas is left.

H5.text: By the end, you will answer both with one small table.

P1.text: The equilibrium constant has three jobs.

P2.text: Job one. Tell us how far the reaction goes.

P3.text: Job two. Tell us which way a mixture will move.

P4.text: Job three. Help us calculate the amounts left at equilibrium.

S1.text: Let's line up real reactions on our molecule bench, from the smallest K to the biggest.

S2.text: Nitrogen and oxygen making nitric oxide at room temperature. K is four point eight times ten to the minus thirty one. Almost nothing happens.

S3.text: Hydrogen iodide at seven hundred kelvin. K is fifty seven. Plenty of both sides.

S4.text: Water from hydrogen and oxygen at five hundred kelvin. K is two point four times ten to the forty seven. Almost all the way.

S5.text: So, a simple rule. K bigger than a thousand, mostly products.

S6.text: K smaller than one thousandth, mostly reactants. In between, a good amount of both.

L1.text: Now job two. Picture a see-saw that balances only at K.

L2.text: At any moment, we write the same fraction with the amounts right now. This is the reaction quotient, Q.

L3.text: If Q is smaller than K, the reaction moves forward. If Q is bigger, it moves backward. If they are equal, it is at equilibrium.

D1.text: Let's test it, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. For two A going to B plus C, K c is two times ten to the minus three.

D3.text: Step two. Right now, A, B and C are each three times ten to the minus four molar.

D4.text: Step three. Q c equals B times C, over A squared. That is exactly one.

D5.text: Step four. One is much bigger than K. So Q must shrink. The reaction runs backward and makes more A.

G1.text: Now job three, finding the amounts. We use a small table with three rows.

G2.text: Row one, Initial. What we start with.

G3.text: Row two, Change. What reacts, written with x, using the balanced equation.

G4.text: Row three, Equilibrium. Start plus change.

G5.text: Then put the last row into K, and solve for x. Students call it the ICE table.

C1.text: Compare. K is the final score. Q is the live score. K stays fixed at one temperature. Q keeps changing until it equals K.

K1.text: Pause and think. Q is ten, and K is fifty seven. Which way does the reaction move?

K2.text: Forward. Q is smaller than K, so more products form until Q grows to fifty seven.

R1.text: One last link, to Gibbs energy.

R2.text: Delta G equals delta G naught, plus R T times the natural log of Q.

R3.text: At equilibrium, delta G is zero and Q equals K. So delta G naught equals minus R T natural log K.

R4.text: If Q is smaller than K, delta G is negative. The forward reaction is spontaneous.

R5.text: If Q is bigger than K, delta G is positive. The backward reaction goes instead.

T1.text: Remember this. Q smaller than K, forward. Q bigger, backward.

W2.text: Three moles of phosphorus pentachloride, P C l five, in a one litre flask at three eighty kelvin, split into P C l three and chlorine. K c is one point eight. Find the amounts.

W3.text: Initial, three molar of P C l five, and zero of the others. Change, minus x, plus x, plus x.

W4.text: Equilibrium, three minus x, x, and x. So x squared over three minus x equals one point eight.

W5.text: Solve. x squared plus one point eight x minus five point four equals zero. x is about one point five nine.

W6.text: So P C l three and chlorine are one point five nine molar each. P C l five is one point four one molar.

X2.text: Students flip the rule. They think a big Q means forward.

X3.text: It is the opposite. A big Q means too much product already. The reaction runs backward.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Boards ask for the direction from Q and K, or the amounts. Entrance tests add a quadratic, or link K to delta G.

Q1.text: Exam level now. For hydrogen and iodine making hydrogen iodide, K c is fifty seven at seven hundred kelvin. A flask has zero point one molar hydrogen, zero point one molar iodine, and zero point seven molar hydrogen iodide. Which way does it move? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Q c is forty nine, so it moves forward.

A2.text: Q c equals hydrogen iodide squared, over hydrogen times iodine.

A3.text: Zero point seven squared is zero point four nine. Divide by zero point zero one. Forty nine.

A4.text: Forty nine is less than fifty seven, so forward. A forgot to square.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. If K is ten to the fifty, what does the mixture mostly hold?

Y3.text: Two. Q is bigger than K. Which way does the reaction move?

Y4.text: Three. What are the three rows of an ICE table?

N1.text: Next time: what happens when we push an equilibrium, by adding gas or heating it? We find out in Le Chatelier's Principle.
